review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Bio-inspired photosynapse hardware with wide spectrum information fusion imaging and neuromorphic processing is promising for complex environment perception. However, integrating ultra-wide spectrum responsivity within a single photosynapse device and scaling to a large array has remained challenging. Here, we demonstrate a 64k-scale (65,536 pixels) ultraviolet-to-mid-infrared photosynapse array based on carbon nanotube/molybdenum oxide heterojunctions. Typical photosynapse behaviors are confirmed in the wide spectrum region of 365 nm (ultraviolet), 532 nm (visible), 1064 nm (near infrared), and 10.6 μm (mid-infrared). A polydopamine-mediated surface treatment enables homogeneous deposition of carbon nanotube/molybdenum oxide films across heterogeneous transistor substrates with 99.96% yield. The photosynapse array enhances image frame similarity from 0.897 to 0.965 in dynamic trajectory prediction. Furthermore, the wide spectrum neuromorphic fusion imaging using photosynapse array achieves 99.58% accuracy in trajectory recognition under challenging conditions, surpassing the 63.93% with visible light alone. This work contributes to paving the way for next-generation autonomous perception.

---

## Introduction

Next-generation autonomous systems require robust perception capabilities in diverse and challenging environments such as haze, fog, and nighttime1,2. These systems must reliably recognize objects, interpret scenes, and predict trajectories to ensure safe navigation and real-time decision-making3,4. Current automotive sensing relies predominantly on visible (Vis) spectrum complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS) sensors. For example, dynamic vision sensors (DVS) have demonstrates impressive performance in challenging conditions5,6. However, these sensors remain limited to the visible spectrum, whereas many critical autonomous navigation scenarios require perception beyond visible wavelengths7–11. In this regard, wide spectrum fusion imaging beyond Vis information offers a promising solution12–14. For example, the fusion of infrared (IR) with Vis imaging provides complementary sensing capabilities when Vis spectrum performance degrades, as IR wavelengths experience reduced Mie scattering in particulate matter such as fog and smoke compared to Vis light, enabling more effective transmission in diverse and challenging environments14.

However, implementing wide spectrum sensing faces significant architectural and device challenges15. The separation between sensing and processing units requires complex preprocessing pipelines for each spectrum band16. A typical pipeline includes sequential stages of sensing, signal conditioning, analog-to-digital conversion (ADC), and data storage/retrieval17. For wide spectrum systems, existing methods primarily require multiple discrete sensors for different spectrum12, necessitating numerous sensor-to-processor pathways that collectively increase physical footprint, power consumption, and system complexity. Additionally, such multi-sensor configurations require sophisticated image algorithms to reconcile the positional misalignment and resolution inconsistencies across different sensor types18. Therefore, there is an urgent need for advanced device and architecture that can simultaneously achieve wide spectrum fusion imaging with efficient in situ processing capabilities.

Fortunately, neuromorphic photosynapse hardware could provide a promising solution for above challenges19. Their synapse-mimicked behaviors enable in situ optical information processing at the pixel level during the sensing process without requiring external circuitry. Recent advances20–35 have already demonstrated their efficacy in ultraviolet (UV) or Vis spectrum, including successful implementations of UV image preprocessing24 and Vis light reservoir computing27. These capabilities have been validated through software-level simulations21,26,27,31,34 or small-scale (typically <32×32) array implementations23–25,28–30,32,33 (Supplementary Table 1), establishing a solid foundation for expanding into the integration of ultra-wide spectrum fusion imaging and energy-efficient neuromorphic processing.

Despite these advances, implementing a large-scale photosynapse array with ultra wide spectrum response, especially extending beyond the current UV-to-Vis range to infrared range, remains challenging. First, it is difficult to realize the synapse temporal dynamics behavior for low-energy photons such as near-infrared (NIR) and mid-infrared (MIR) because the high background of thermally-excited carriers in narrowband gap semiconductors leads to rapid carrier recombination. Second, scaling a single device to a large-scale array is hindered by surface energy mismatches between heterogeneous-surface transistor readout circuitry and active materials, resulting in compositional heterogeneity and compromised device-to-device performance consistency.

Here, we demonstrate a 64k (65536 pixels)-scale UV-to-MIR photosynapse array based on carbon nanotube/molybdenum oxide (CNT/MoO3) heterojunctions. The photocarriers in narrow bandgap CNT undergo band alignment-assisted vacancy carrier trapping in MoO3, facilitating the synapse-mimicking dynamics (Fig. 1a). Typical photosynapse response behaviors are confirmed in the wide spectrum region of 365 nm (UV), 532 nm (Vis), 1064 nm (NIR), and 10.6 μm (MIR), respectively. A polydopamine-mediated treatment renders heterogeneous transistor substrate surfaces homogeneous, facilitating CNT/MoO3 film deposition and contributing the high-yield photosynapse array. The demonstrated array exhibits the wide spectrum response range and the high integration scale compared to previously reported photosynapse results (Fig. 1b, c, Supplementary Table 1). The neuromorphic information processing capacity in photosynapse hardware improves dynamic trajectory prediction tasks with image similarity from 0.897 to 0.965 compared to conventional photosensor device. Additionally, the fusion imaging of Vis and MIR achieves an accuracy of 99.58% in trajectory recognition under challenging environmental conditions, outperforming the 63.93% accuracy achieved when using Vis light alone. This integration of wide spectrum sensing and neuromorphic processing in a large-scale array represents a significant advance in hardware-based visual information processing, offering promising possibilities for robust perception systems in diverse and challenging operational environments.

---

## Results

Design of ultra-wide spectrum photosynapse device
To integrate wide spectrum sensing with neuromorphic processing, we design a photosynapse device based on CNT/MoO3 heterojunctions. As illustrated in Fig. 1a, the device features a vertical paradigm with an indium tin oxide (ITO) electrode and a CNT/MoO3 active layer, where CNT conductive pathways with dispersed MoO3 nanoparticles creating heterojunctions interfaces. This design utilizes complementary material properties: the narrow bandgap of CNT enables effective absorption from UV to MIR region, while the wide bandgap MoO3 with abundant oxygen vacancy defect states provides ultraviolet response and carrier trapping dynamics.

The preparation of CNT/MoO3 film employed water-based processes (see Methods for details), which has potential for large-scale integration in subsequent sections. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) reveals well-defined crystalline domains of MoO3 with lattice spacing of 0.230 nm (Supplementary Fig. 1)36, which is in agreement with X-ray diffraction patterns (Supplementary Fig. 2a). Raman spectroscopy provides further confirmation of the hybrid material composition. The CNT/MoO3 composite exhibited characteristic Raman peaks at 820 cm⁻¹ and 995 cm⁻¹, attributed to the stretching modes of Mo-O-Mo and Mo=O bonds in MoO3, respectively37 (Supplementary Fig. 2b). The characteristic G-band (1590 cm⁻¹) and D-band (1350 cm⁻¹) signatures of CNT were also clearly resolved37. These results demonstrate that CNT/MoO3 films were successfully prepared using water-based method.

Fabrication of large-scale photosynapse array
Large-scale photosynapse array fabrication faces primary challenges originating from substrate heterogeneity, which significantly impacts device uniformity across arrays (Fig. 2a). For example, standard CMOS or thin film transistor (TFT) platforms typically feature heterogeneous surfaces comprising passivation layers (e.g., SiOx, SiNx) and patterned electrodes38,39 (e.g., Cu metal, ITO), which create material interfaces with distinct surface properties. To investigate this issue, we fabricated TFT array structures following standard semiconductor processing protocols, with ITO electrode arrays and SiNx passivation layers as the critical top interface materials. Detailed fabrication processes are provided in the Supplementary Fig. 3 and Supplementary Note 1. As illustrated in Fig. 2b, the original substrates exhibit significant water contact angle disparities between ITO (~42.9±2.1°) and SiNx (~84.5±2.5°) region (mean±standard deviation). These interfacial contact angle disparities compromise film integrity during CNT/MoO3 deposition, resulting in uneven material distribution across material interfaces and crack formation on surfaces with higher contact angles. Figure 2c reveals characteristic cracking patterns on unmodified SiNx surfaces, highlighting the demand for surface treatment strategy.

We propose polydopamine (PDA) modification as an effective solution to this problem. PDA is a catecholamine-derived polymer with strong adhesive properties that forms robust interfacial bonds with various substrate surfaces38,39. The PDA modification procedure is detailed in the Methods section. In contrast to original substrate, PDA-treated surfaces demonstrate consistent contact angles on ITO (27.0±1.6°) and SiNx (25.0±3.0°), with substantially reduced contact angles compared to their initial states, facilitating uniform material deposition. The materials deposited after polydopamine treatment exhibit crack-free characteristics (Fig. 2c), maintaining uniformity even at the ITO-SiNx interface regions (Supplementary Fig. 4).

The underlying mechanism for this uniformity enhancement was characterized. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis confirms effective binding between PDA and the heterogeneous substrate surfaces. On SiNx substrates, the Si 2p peak exhibits characteristic broadening and a positive shift in binding energy after PDA modification (Supplementary Fig. 5a), suggesting the effective interaction between SiNx and PDA40. Similarly, for ITO surfaces, the Sn 3d5/2 peak shows an increased binding energy from 486.5 eV to 486.7 eV after PDA modification (Supplementary Fig. 5b), confirming interfacial interaction between ITO and PDA41. The uniform contact angle achieved across heterogeneous ITO/SiNx substrates originates from this interfacial adhesion capability and PDA intrinsic surface properties38,39. The deposited PDA layer presents abundant surface functional groups such as quinone and secondary amines, which dictate its uniform wetting behavior24. The contact angle remained stable after 30 days of ambient storage (Supplementary Fig. 6), illustrating the good stability of PDA modification. Optical characterization shows PDA absorption spanning UV to MIR wavelengths. However, in the UV-Vis-NIR regions, photogenerated carriers suffer from poor transport in the amorphous polymer42,43, while MIR absorption induces molecular vibrations without carrier generation, indicating limited contribution to the photoelectric response. XPS analysis of Mo 3d spectra shows nearly identical Mo5+/Mo6+ ratios (1:2.03 vs 1:2.05) with and without PDA modification. These results indicate that PDA functions primarily as a surface modifier without significantly altering the photoelectronic properties of the active layers (see detailed analysis in Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Figs. 7, 8).

To evaluate the reliability and scalability of our PDA modification approach, we characterized the electrical uniformity of medium-scale (4k-scale, 4096 pixels) and large-scale (64k-scale, 65536 pixels) photosynapse arrays based on dark current relative non-uniformity (DCRNU), photo response non-uniformity (PRNU) and Moran’s I index analysis. DCRNU reflects the pixel-to-pixel variation in dark current normalized to the mean dark signal, which is defined as:
DCRNU = (σ_dark / μ_dark) * 100% (1)
where σ_dark is the standard deviation of dark current across all pixels, and μ_dark is the mean dark current. PRNU reflects the pixel-to-pixel variation in photo response normalized to the effective signal, which is defined as:
PRNU = (σ_photo / μ_photo - μ_dark) * 100% (2)
where σ_photo is the standard deviation of photocurrent, μ_photo is the mean photocurrent, and μ_dark is the mean dark current. Moran’s I index reflects the spatial autocorrelation of pixel current across the array, which is defined as:
I_Moran = (N / W) * (Σ_i,j w_ij (I_pixel,i - I_pixel_mean) * (I_pixel,j - I_pixel_mean)) / (Σ_i (I_pixel,i - I_pixel_mean)^2) (3)
where N is the total number of pixels, I_pixel is the pixel current value, I_pixel_mean is the mean current. We used a queen contiguity configuration where pixels sharing edges or corners are considered adjacent. The spatial weight w_ij was defined using a queen contiguity configuration where pixels sharing edges or corners were assigned a value of 1 and 0 otherwise, with W representing the sum of all weights.

As illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 9, the 4k array under dark conditions demonstrates a mean current of 34.6±1.2 nA with a DCRNU of 3.4%. Spatial correlation analysis yielded a Moran’s I index of 0.3010 for dark current, indicating moderate spatial clustering and good electrical uniformity. The calculated PRNU yielded 13.2% for the 4k array. All pixels in the 4k array were functional, resulting in 100% yield. Figure 2d, f showed the dark current and current spatial distribution and statistical result of the 64k array, respectively. The 64k array showed a mean dark current of 7.9±0.8 nA with the DCRNU of 10.1%. The Moran’s I indices of 0.3010 (64×64 array) and 0.7613 (256×256 array) indicate that the dark current is distributed randomly across the array, with no significant spatial clustering (see Supplementary Note 3 for detailed analysis). These edge effects caused by topographical variations where interconnects route to peripheral pads, become more pronounced in larger arrays, as supported by the spatial clustering of failed pixels in edge regions (Supplementary Fig. 10). Future potential improvements include optimized peripheral routing topology to minimize edge effect, combined with adaptive non-uniformity correction (NUC) algorithms employing two-point calibration or scene-based statistical methods to compensate for residual fixed-pattern noise44,45.

Figure 2e, f exhibited the light current spatial distribution and statistical result, respectively. The calculated PRNU was 27.7% under illumination at 532 nm, which is comparable to the variability observed in conventional CMOS image sensors46. The corresponding PRNU values at 365 nm, 1064 nm, and 10.6 μm were 27.3%, 29.4%, and 30.2%, respectively (see Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Note 4 for details). These results confirm the PDA modification approach for reliable large-scale photosynapse array integration (Fig. 2g).

Characterization of ultra-wide spectrum photosynapse
The as-proposed CNT/MoO3 device demonstrates photosynapse behaviors across an ultra-wide spectrum from UV to MIR wavelengths. As shown in Fig. 3a-b, under a series of ten consecutive optical pulse stimulation of 10.6 μm MIR (0.25 Hz, ON/OFF=2s/2s), the post-synapse current exhibits progressive enhancement with subsequent pulses. A saturation effect is observed in the post-synapse current, where the current increment gradually diminishes with subsequent pulses until reaching a plateau. This saturation behavior is analogous to the depletion of readily releasable neurotransmitter vesicle pools in biological synapses, where continued stimulation leads to diminishing postsynapse responses until vesicle recycling occurs47,48. Following cessation of the optical pulse train, the photoresponse exhibits a gradual decay profile, analogous to the retention characteristics of biological synapses49,50. When the stimulation frequency increases to 0.5 Hz (ON/OFF=1s/1s, Supplementary Fig. 11), the short inter-pulse intervals prevent complete current decay between pulses, resulting in accumulation of successive current responses. This photoresponse mimics low-pass filtering properties characteristic of biological synaptic dynamics, where the exponential decay creates a temporal integration window that preferentially transmits low-frequency signals while attenuating high-frequency components49. Such behavior differs from conventional photoconductive devices, which typically exhibit static photoresponse without history-dependent modulation.

Figure 3c–f presents the post-synapse current behavior of the device under dual-pulse stimulation with varying time intervals across different wavelengths, all exhibiting significant paired-pulse facilitation effects.

To evaluate the linearity and dynamic range of our photosynapse devices, we characterized the intensity-dependent photoresponse across the wide spectrum range (Supplementary Figs. 15, 16). Detailed wavelength-dependent responsivity measurements demonstrate effective wide-spectrum photoresponse from UV to MIR range (Supplementary Fig. 15). The photocurrent exhibits a sublinear power-law dependence on incident optical power (I_ph ∝ P^α) with α < 1 across all tested wavelengths from UV to MIR, suggesting trap-related photoresponse processes51 (see Supplementary Note 6 for detailed analysis). Device-to-device uniformity measurements demonstrate consistent photosynapse behavior (Fig. 3l and Supplementary Fig. 17).

These results suggest robust photosynapse functionality across an ultra-wide spectrum range covering UV to MIR. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the widest spectrum coverage exceeding previously reported ranges for photosynapse devices (Fig. 3g, Supplementary Table 1). This wide spectrum photoresponse spanning visible to 10.6 μm wavelengths suggests that our photosynapse device could potentially simplify multiple imaging sensors such as RGB and IR camera in autonomous vehicles into a single device, reducing system complexity while maintaining multi-spectrum perception capabilities52,53. Besides, the device exhibits low power consumption of 23.9 nW per pixel at 0.5 V bias (Supplementary Note 8), demonstrating potential for energy-efficient perception systems.

To understand this exceptional performance, we characterized the electronic and optical properties of photosynapse device. XPS analysis demonstrates the coexistence of Mo6+ and Mo5+ oxidation states27 (Fig. 3h) and three distinct oxygen environments32 (Fig. 3i), confirming oxygen vacancy traps within the MoO354,55. Optical measurements reveal complementary absorption properties for ultra-wide spectrum response. UV-Vis spectroscopy and tauc plot analysis show 3.3 eV indirect bandgap56 of MoO3 with characteristic oxygen vacancy trap-assisted absorption36 at ~600 nm (Fig. 2j). Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and tauc plot fitting results confirm a narrow direct bandgap of 0.094 eV in CNT (Fig. 2k), which is consistent with previous literature57.

Since MIR radiation can induce thermal effects through absorption in device components including active materials, substrate and ITO electrodes (Supplementary Fig. 19), we conducted systematic experiments to investigate the contribution of thermally-induced conductivity changes for synapse behaviors. Thermal imaging of the entire device under operating conditions reveals a temperature rise of 2.8 K during MIR illumination, contributing ~1.2 nA to the total photocurrent. (Supplementary Fig. 20). Pulse-train experiments support that synaptic plasticity originates from photocarrier trapping rather than thermal accumulation (Supplementary Fig. 21), with stable ohmic contacts maintained within the temperature range. Detailed analysis of these thermal effects is provided in Supplementary Note 7. Based on these results, we can elucidate the mechanism underlying the observed photosynapse behavior. Upon illumination, incident photons are absorbed primarily by CNT across the ultra-wide spectrum (UV to MIR) due to the narrow bandgap, while MoO3 contributes significantly to absorption in the UV region. The work function difference between MoO3 (6.16 eV) and CNT (3.92 eV) creates an asymmetric interfacial energy landscape (see more detailed band alignment measurement in Supplementary Note 5) that drives photoexcited electrons from CNT to MoO3 upon illumination58,59. These electrons are subsequently captured by oxygen vacancy traps in MoO3. This process of band alignment-driven carrier transfer and oxygen vacancies mediated carrier trapping creates an electrostatic field that effectively modulates carrier concentration in adjacent CNT channels, producing the observed photosynapse dynamics. The wavelength-dependent decay differences can be attributed to the influence of carrier generation mechanisms and trap states filling levels. Higher-energy UV and Vis photons generate carriers in both CNTs and MoO3, leading to efficient trap filling and faster trap-assisted recombination with relatively short decay time constants60,61. In contrast, MIR photons (10.6 μm) generate relatively low-density carriers only through narrow-bandgap CNT absorption, resulting in partial trap filling and slower detrapping as well as recombination processes with extended decay times62. Additionally, MIR illumination induces a local temperature rise (Supplementary Fig. 19), and the thermal relaxation after illumination cessation may further contribute to the extended decay63. This photosynapse device with moderate time constants is suitable for applications without stringent speed requirements while benefiting from memory effects.

Demonstration of static and dynamic imaging
The ultra-wide spectrum photosynapse array with large-scale enables direct hardware-level imaging. To demonstrate this capability, we investigated the array performance in differentiating materials with varied spectrum absorption characteristics. When imaging complex multi-material objects, wide spectrum approaches reveal compositional details that remain indistinguishable under single-wavelength illumination18. As illustrated in Fig. 4a, certain materials exhibit strong absorption under ultraviolet light, while in the visible range, these same materials show distinctive contrast patterns that enable detailed discrimination.

We conducted experimental validation using two distinct glass container types: transparent borosilicate glass and transition metal oxide-doped UV-opaque glass. Both containers incorporated metallic ring inclusions. The experimental configurations, including embedded metallic ring and encapsulating glass, are documented in Fig. 4b, e. Comparative imaging analysis under 365 nm UV and 532 nm Vis illumination reveals distinct characteristics. Group I exhibited similar object visibility across both spectral regions (Fig. 4c, f). In contrast, Group II displayed marked wavelength-dependent behavior: 365 nm UV imaging reveals only exterior morphology due to strong surface absorption, while 532 nm Vis imaging (Fig. 4d, g) enabled clear visualization of internal metallic components. These results demonstrate that wide spectrum imaging provides more comprehensive object information, enabling detection of concealed components that remain insufficiently contrasted under limited-spectrum illumination. Furthermore, raster-scanning imaging in the MIR (1064 nm) and MIR (10.6 μm) regions yielded well-resolved patterns (Supplementary Fig. 22), confirming the array’s imaging functionality across the ultra-wide spectrum range. Passive thermal imaging of room-temperature objects without external illumination, however, remains challenging. This limitation may be attributed to the relatively large noise from residual metallic CNTs and 1/f noise in amorphous silicon TFTs. Potential strategies include achieving higher semiconducting CNT purity through advanced sorting techniques64, and integrating silicon CMOS readout circuits65 for improved noise performance.

Beyond static imaging, the photosynapse array offers advantages in dynamic scene analysis through its inherent spatial-temporal response characteristics. Exponential decay-based temporal encoding is well-established in neuromorphic vision systems66. Our photosynapse implements this principle across the UV-to-MIR spectrum in hardware through stimulus-dependent conductance retention and gradual photocurrent decay. This intrinsic integration function creates a system where current amplitude directly indicates stimulus recency, with recently activated pixels maintaining higher states while earlier activated regions exhibit progressive attenuation. Consequently, each frame inherently encodes a time-weighted history of motion trajectories. The wide-spectrum photosynapse array have the potential for trajectory tracking both visible and non-visible dynamic features. Moreover, our photosynapse architecture offers the potential to avoid temporal surface reconstruction, as the accumulated conductance state can be directly readout, simplifying prediction tasks that would otherwise require reconstructing temporal surfaces from event streams.

We quantified this advantage using a cycle-consistent generative adversarial network (CycleGAN) framework67,68 that exploits embedded temporal correlations. As shown in Fig. 5b. The architecture employs bidirectional generator-discriminator pairs that map between sequential states (t→t+1, t+1→t), maintaining trajectory physics constraints through cycle consistency mechanisms. To isolate temporal integration effects, we established two comparative datasets: photosynapse trajectories captured using precision-controlled laser stimulation (Fig. 5c) and simulated conventional sensor responses created through Hadamard product operations. The latter preserved only current position information while eliminating historical context, effectively replicating traditional sensors without persistent states.

We employed the Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) to quantitatively evaluate prediction fidelity. The higher SSIM values indicating better preservation of structural information. Photosynapse-based prediction achieved a significantly higher SSIM value of 0.965±0.018 between predicted and ground truth frames, compared to 0.897±0.032 for conventional approaches (Fig. 5d), representing an improvement in prediction accuracy. Frame analysis (Fig. 5e–j) demonstrates trajectory prediction capabilities comparing photosynapse and conventional sensor approaches. The photosynapse input (Fig. 5e) exhibits intrinsic temporal integration through visible trajectory trails, while conventional sensor input (Fig. 5h) captures only current position information. When compared to real next frames (Fig. 5f, i), predictions based on photosynapse image maintain trajectory coherence and spatial accuracy (Fig. 5g), whereas conventional sensor predictions (Fig. 5j) show reduced fidelity with motion path deviation.

Demonstration of neuromorphic fusion imaging
Following our investigation of dynamic trajectory prediction capabilities, we examined the critical challenge of maintaining perception reliability in adverse environmental conditions. We developed an experimental platform specifically designed to evaluate wide spectrum fusion imaging under simulated atmospheric attenuation. The setup utilized wavelength-dependent laser beam trajectories (10.6 μm MIR and 532 nm Vis) as representative signals for vehicle motion, with an optical filter serving as an analog for atmospheric interference effects such as fog, haze, or smoke (Fig. 6a). These conditions typically attenuate visible light transmission while permitting greater penetration of infrared wavelengths.

The wide spectrum capability of our photosynapse array allows for enhanced perception through fusion imaging, where information from multiple wavelengths (λ1, λ2, …, λk) contributes to a comprehensive representation. The fusion process combines these inputs according to:
I(i,j,fusion) = Σ w_k * I(i,j,λ_k) (4)
where I(i,j,fusion) represents the fused pixel value at position (i,j), w_k represent the relative contribution weight of each wavelength, and I(i,j,λ_k) is the pixel value at position (i,j) for wavelength λ_k.

The experimental protocol incorporated straight and turn trajectory patterns as classification targets, evaluating different imaging configurations: photosynapse array with visible light only (Fig. 6b), photosynapse array with wide spectrum fusion (MIR+Vis) (Fig. 6c) (See Method for details). To ensure fair comparison between photosynapse neuromorphic imaging and conventional hardware imaging capabilities, we constructed parallel datasets by applying a Hadamard product between photosynapse imaging data and binary masks of light spot positions (Supplementary Fig. 23, Supplementary Note 2), effectively preserving spatial information while neutralizing the temporal dynamics advantage.

Performance analysis reveals significant advantages of wide spectrum fusion imaging in challenging environments. Representative wide spectrum neuromorphic fusion images of last frame were presented in Fig. 6d. Learning curves demonstrates that photosynapse hardware utilizing both Vis and MIR wavelengths achieved substantially higher classification accuracy compared to Vis-only sensing under identical environmental conditions (Fig. 6e). Notably, even when both systems utilized the same wavelength fusion, the photosynapse array outperformed conventional hardware by ~37% (Supplementary Fig. 24). Two-fold cross-validation with six parallel tests confirm these findings, with confusion matrices revealing classification accuracies of 99.58% for photosynapse fusion imaging compared to only 63.93% for Vis-only imaging (Fig. 6f, g). To assess classification stability, we evaluated the recognition performance across 10 independent training runs with different random weight initializations (Supplementary Fig. 25). The consistent high accuracy (99.75% ± 0.75%) suggests that images captured by our photosynapse array support stable classification performance. Further analysis of different MIR:Vis fusion ratios showed that classification performance improved with increasing MIR contribution and stabilized at high accuracy level, confirming the robustness of the fusion approach (Supplementary Figs. 26, 27). To further evaluate the contribution of visible-light fusion under various atmospheric conditions, we analyzed our system’ performance using the M3FD dataset with visibility-dependent attenuation based on established atmospheric transmission models69,70. The results demonstrate that wide-spectrum fusion consistently enhances classification accuracy compared to MIR-only imaging across different visibility conditions, suggesting the contribution of visible-light features even under atmospheric attenuation.

We further evaluated performance comparison of our photosynapse array with DVS cameras66,70–72 (see Supplementary Note 11 for details). Under good visibility (100 km), both systems achieve comparable performance (Supplementary Fig. 29). However, under low visibility conditions (1 km), DVS-based methods experience significant performance degradation (accuracy drops to 66.7%~79.2%), as atmospheric attenuation reduces the contrast in visible wavelengths that DVS sensors rely on for event generation73,74. In contrast, our photosynapse array with fused Visible and MIR maintains 97.9% accuracy by utilizing the better penetration of MIR wavelengths through atmospheric obscurants. This demonstrates that the wide-spectrum photosynapse array can complement visible DVS systems by maintaining robust classification in challenging conditions, suggesting potential for combined systems that utilize both technologies’ strengths in future applications.

---

## Methods

Preparation of CNT/MoO3 film
MoO3 nanoparticles were synthesized via a low-temperature oxidation method. A hydrogen peroxide solution (10 mL H2O2 and 20 mL deionized water) was added dropwise to molybdenum powder (0.0417 mol) under continuous magnetic stirring to ensure effective reaction. The reaction was maintained at room temperature under static conditions for 96 h to facilitate complete reaction. The as-synthesized MoO3 dispersion was then mixed with multi-walled carbon nanotube aqueous solution (1wt%) in a volume ratio of 1:1. The mixed MoO3/CNT precursor solution was used for subsequent deposition.

Process of PDA modification on heterogenous substrate
The polydopamine (PDA) coatings on heterogenous substrate through a CuSO4/H2O2-catalyzed oxidation process. The reaction solution was formulated by dissolving dopamine hydrochloride at a concentration of 2 mg mL−1 in a 50 mM Tris buffer solution (pH 8.5) containing 5 mM CuSO4 and 19.6 mM H2O2. The substrates were immersed in the precursor solution for 5 min for PDA deposition. Following immersion, the samples were thoroughly cleaned with deionized water and dried under vacuum at 30 °C for 4 h to remove residual moisture.

Material and device characterization
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurement was conducted on Shimadzu Corporation (AXIS Supra). Raman spectrum was using HORIBA Corporation (HR800) under 532 nm laser excitation. The 10.6 μm light source utilized a Synrad Model 48-1 CO2 laser; the 1064 nm light source employed a Coherent Compass 1064–4000 Nd:YAG laser; the 532 nm light source used a Spectra-Physics Navigator X15SC-532Q frequency-doubled laser; and the 365 nm light source was provided by a Zolix MLED4-3 UV LED system. The electrical performance characterization of the devices was conducted using an Agilent B1500 A measurement system. Signal readout of photosynapse array was evaluated using a self-constructed electrical readout system.

Widespectrum fusion imaging platform and algorithm
An experimental platform was constructed utilizing double lasers operating at 532 nm (visible) and 10.6 μm (mid-infrared) wavelengths. A programmable motorized two-axis stage generated precise linear and curvilinear motion patterns to simulate vehicle movement trajectories. Atmospheric haze conditions were simulated by positioning a germanium filter along the optical path, which selectively attenuated visible wavelengths while maintaining infrared transmission. Image acquisition was implemented through a multiplexed column readout scheme with Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-controlled row-by-row sequential addressing at a frame rate of 12.5 fps (80 ms frame interval, 4k scale array). Precise temporal coordination between row addressing sequences and column multiplexing protocols was maintained to ensure signal integrity throughout the acquisition process. Following digitization, the data was transferred to the host computing system for subsequent analysis. The 532 nm (visible) and 10.6 μm (mid-infrared) images were fused using weighting coefficients of w(532 nm) = w(10.6 μm) = 0.5. For trajectory classification, a convolutional neural network (CNN) was trained on a dataset comprising terminal frames from linear and rotational movement sequences (20 images per category). The CNN consisted of three sequential convolutional blocks (8, 16, and 32 filters, respectively), each followed by batch normalization, ReLU activation, and max pooling operations. The network terminated with a fully connected layer and softmax classification layer. Training employed 5-fold cross-validation using stochastic gradient descent with momentum (SGDM) optimization and 500 training epochs. Performance was evaluated using validation accuracy metrics and confusion matrices.

Calculation of SSIM
The SSIM measures image similarity by:
SSIM(x,y) = ((2μ_x μ_y + C1)(2σ_xy + C2)) / ((μ_x^2 + μ_y^2 + C1)(σ_x^2 + σ_y^2 + C2)) (5)
where μ_x and μ_y are the means of images X and Y, σ_x and σ_y are their standard deviations, σ_xy is the covariance of images X and Y, and C1, C2 are non-negative regularization parameters that prevent divisional instability.

Data availability
Fusion image data used for comparison is pre-processed from the publicly available M3FD dataset69. All data supporting the key findings of this study are available within the article and its Supplementary Information files. Source data are provided with this paper. Additional raw data are available from the corresponding authors upon request. Source data are provided with this paper.

Code availability
The codes for plotting the data are available from the corresponding author upon request.

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript entitled “Ultra-Wide Spectrum Photosynapse Array with 64k-Scale for Neuromorphic Fusion Imaging” by
Dun et al. presents a technical advance in the field of neuromorphic vision. The authors report the fabrication of a 64k-scale
photosynapse array utilizing a polydopamine-mediated process to achieve a device yield of 99.96%, addressing a
scalability bottleneck in neuromorphic optoelectronic hardware. The use of CNT/MoO₃ heterojunctions enables a broadband
spectral response, ranging from the ultraviolet (365 nm) to the long-wave infrared (10.6 μm), facilitating spatiotemporal data
integration directly at the sensor level. This hardware-level fusion removes the need for complex multi-sensor post-
processing and enhances motion prediction accuracy and scene understanding. The manuscript is generally well structured,
and the experimental results are convincing. However, I would recommend acceptance after addressing the following minor
but important technical clarifications and experimental validations.
1. The authors report a high functional yield of 99.96% in the 64k-array, with only 23 pixels identified as non-functional.
While this demonstrates excellent fabrication uniformity, further discussion of the failure analysis is necessary. Specifically,
please provide a spatial map or statistical analysis of the defect distribution. Are the defective pixels clustered in specific
regions (e.g., edges, corners), or are they randomly distributed across the array? Such analysis could help identify process
sensitivities or systematic fabrication deviations that could guide future yield optimization.
2. In Figure 6e, the manuscript presents learning curves for recognition tasks. However, as training in neuromorphic systems
is often sensitive to initial conditions, especially in hardware-accelerated platforms, it is important to assess the stability of
convergence. Please conduct and report recognition performance using multiple initial random weight configurations.
Present quantitative metrics such as standard deviation of final accuracy and number of epochs to convergence across
trials. These results can be included in the Supporting Information and would substantiate the robustness of the training
process.
3. The manuscript describes a dual-modal fusion imaging strategy integrating mid-infrared (MIR) and visible (Vis) signals. To
further substantiate the benefit of adaptive modality fusion, please perform experiments varying the MIR:Vis weighting ratios
(e.g., 0.3:0.7, 0.4:0.6, 0.6:0.4, 0.7:0.3). Report classification accuracy for motion patterns under each weighting condition, and
provide corresponding confusion matrices. This parametric analysis would offer valuable insight into the system’s tolerance
to signal imbalance and help characterize the optimal fusion configuration.
4. To enable a deeper understanding of the device physics and to facilitate comparisons with prior art, please provide
detailed responsivity data across the various wavelength range of interest. It is also important to specify the ambient or
controlled temperature at which these measurements were conducted, as temperature can significantly influence the
responsivity of infrared and broadband photodetectors. Inclusion of this data—either in the main text or as Supporting
Information—would improve the reproducibility and interpretability of the results.
5. The system is suitable for real-time autonomous perception. No data are provided on power consumption per pixel. For
neuromorphic vision applications in autonomous systems, energy are key performance indicators.
6. Only a few pulse-response traces are shown per wavelength, and decay behaviors are fitted with biexponential curves.
However, statistical variability across multiple devices or pixels is not reported.
7. The manuscript uses multiple phrases to describe the surface treatment process, including “polydopamine modification,”
“PDA treatment,” and “polydopamine surface modification technique.” For clarity and consistency, please unify the
terminology throughout the manuscript. If abbreviations are used (e.g., PDA), ensure that they are clearly defined at first
mention and used uniformly thereafter. A standardized nomenclature would enhance the professional presentation and
readability of the work.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript demonstrates a neuromorphic vision hardware consisting of a 64k-scale ultraviolet-to-mid-infrared (UV-to-
MIR) photosynapse array based on CNT/MoO3 heterojunctions, which achieves 99.58% classification accuracy in trajectory
recognition through wide-spectrum neuromorphic fusion imaging. The development of large-scale neuromorphic arrays and
broadband imaging systems is of considerable significance for robust perception in complex environments. However, the
manuscript lacks in-depth mechanistic exploration of broadband response and synaptic dynamics, which limits its instructive
value for the field. I encourage the authors to carefully address the following major concerns before I can support its
publication.
1. The authors report photoresponse non-uniformity (PRNU) only in the visible range. To support the claimed ultra-wide
spectral responsivity, the PRNU characterization should be extended to UV, NIR, and MIR regions. This would provide a
more comprehensive understanding of device uniformity across the full operational spectrum.
2. Unclear synaptic behavior under MIR stimulation (Figure 3b). Under repeated MIR pulses, the post-synaptic current
exhibits inconsistent peaks (alternating high and low responses), which is inconsistent with typical synaptic facilitation
behavior. Detailed experimental parameters, including optical pulse intensity, duration, and number, should be clearly
stated. Additionally, further analysis is needed to clarify the origin of the observed saturation behavior and whether it reflects
a true synaptic dynamic or a conventional photoconductive response.
3. The manuscript lacks detailed experimental evidence to distinguish between photothermal and photoconductive
contributions in the MIR response of CNT. Given that mid-infrared radiation typically induces thermal effects, the authors
should perform control experiments (e.g., with modulated MIR sources, temperature monitoring, or thermal shielding) to
verify whether the observed MIR response arises from photocarrier generation or thermal conductivity changes.
4. Although the device is claimed to operate from UV to MIR, the authors only present static imaging demonstrations in the
UV and visible ranges. The absence of NIR and MIR imaging experiments raises questions about the device performance in
these bands. Are there limitations in sensitivity that preclude demonstration in the infrared? Clarification is required.
5. In Figure 6b, the visible-light trajectory is barely distinguishable from the background under the simulated haze
environment. The authors should quantify the transmission of visible light through the attenuation medium used in the
experimental setup. Given the poor visibility in the visible range, it is plausible that MIR imaging alone could yield near-perfect classification accuracy, potentially diminishing the added value of spectral fusion.
6. The authors should clarify the MIR transmittance of their ITO films and whether MIR-induced heating affects the electrical
conductivity or contact properties of the device, potentially altering its responsivity.
7. Polydopamine (PDA) is used as a surface modifier to improve film uniformity. The authors should clarify whether PDA
exhibits any optical absorption in the UV-to-MIR range or contributes defect states at the CNT/MoO3 or interface that may
affect the photosynaptic behavior.
8. Figure 1a schematically illustrates the band alignment between CNT and MoO3 but does not provide direct experimental
or theoretical support. The authors should indicate how this alignment was determined.
9. The authors show double-exponential decay times (Figure 3l) that increase with wavelength. In particular, MIR responses
exhibit much slower decay than UV–Vis. Is this due to different carrier dynamics or trap distributions? A more detailed
discussion of wavelength-dependent dynamics is warranted, especially for synaptic applications requiring high-speed
response.
10. The manuscript lacks light-intensity-dependent responsivity data. This information is critical to evaluate linearity,
dynamic range, and potential gain effects under different optical power levels across spectral bands. Such measurements
would also help distinguish synaptic accumulation from trap saturation effects.
11. Given that thermal radiation from real-world targets at room temperature peaks near 10 μm, the authors should discuss
whether their array can effectively image dynamic thermal scenes without external illumination. Demonstrating passive MIR
detection at room temperature would significantly strengthen the practical impact of the work.

### Reviewer 3

The authors present a 64k-scale photosynapse array based on CNT/MoO3 heterojunctions for neuromorphic vision
applications. The device demonstrates ultra-wide spectral response from UV to MIR and achieves high fabrication yield
through polydopamine surface modification. The demonstrated improvements in trajectory prediction and recognition
accuracy under challenging conditions are encouraging. The manuscript is generally well-organized and the experimental

(1) The authors demonstrate that polydopamine treatment improves device uniformity. To further strengthen the discussion

(2) The authors state that the Moran’s I index increases from 0.3010 (4k array) to 0.7613 (64k array), indicating enhanced

(3) The authors mention using a “queen contiguity configuration” for Moran’s I calculation without explanation. Please
provide a brief clarification of this spatial weight matrix configuration for readers unfamiliar with spatial statistics terminology.
(4) The authors report achieving 99.96% pixel yield in the 64k array. It would be helpful if the authors could provide a spatial
map or brief description of the non-functional pixel distribution to understand whether defects are randomly distributed or
show clustering patterns.
(5) In Figure 4 caption, there appears to be a typographical error. “365 nm visible light” and “532 nm UV light” should be

### Reviewer 4

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature

### Reviewer 5

The authors present a wide-spectrum photosynapse array based on CNT/MoO3 heterojunction with the largest
demonstrated array size and response spectrum. A compelling case for wide response spectrum is made with side-by-side
comparison of a glass bottle containing a metal ring that is imaged using UV light and visible light. Both imaging results are

array shows strong potential for realizing a wide-spectrum combined sensing + processing system applied to
learning/robotics.
The following comments and questions are provided with regard to this work:
1. In Line 48-51, authors mention that visible spectrum + CMOS sensors perform poorly in adverse visibility conditions.
Currently, dynamic vision sensors (DVS), which transmit sparse, event-driven spikes, also offer heightened computer vision
(CV) performance in challenging conditions, like fog and smoke, due to higher temporal resolution, reduced motion blur, and
logarithmic light sensitivity (and therefore high dynamic range) when compared to RGB cameras. See
https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.08405 and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.10540 for more details. Additionally, due to DVS emulating the
retina, they are well-suited to integrate into neuromorphic systems that aim to unite brain-like computation and brain-like
sensory peripherals. Lastly, there is an established community of neuromorphic CV and robotics engineers that have
designed and optimized software packages, like LavaDL (for Loihi 2 simulation/programming) and Neuromorphic
Intermediate Representation (connecting LavaDL, snnTorch, SpiNNaker2, Norse, etc.), for a streamlined DVS to
computational hardware to learning/robotics pipeline. How does the proposed photosynapse array compare with DVS/event
cameras? Specifically, what tasks would the proposed system outperform an RGB + DVS system and what is the
frequency/criticality of such tasks (e.g., in the context of autonomous vehicles)?
2. I can see how the proposed photosynapse array has strong potential to simplify existing sensing/computing systems.
However, I would like to see a clearer connection made here. Namely, existing autonomous systems use a suite of sensors,
including LiDAR, radar, RGB camera, IR/thermal. What portion of this sensor suite would the proposed system simplify?
3. In Line 191, a Moran’s I index of 0.3010 for dark current is mentioned. This suggests there is some spatial correlations in
the visual scene. Is this from some fixed-pattern noise, thermal leakage, or electrical crosstalk between nearby devices?
Additionally, in Line 197, was the higher Moran’s I index of 0.7613 also in dark conditions? Am I correct in my understanding
that Moran’s I index should be close to zero in dark conditions? If not, could this be clarified more in the manuscript?
4. In Line 220-222, it is stated that the frequency-dependent photoresponse (i.e., the extent of synaptic relaxation/leakage)
mimics the temporal filtering properties of biological neural systems, allowing neural circuits to selectively respond to
specific temporal frequencies of input signals. It is very unclear how this is possible. My best guess is that synaptic
decay/Laplace kernels act as low-pass filters (e.g., a Lorentzian-style frequency response) which allow only certain
frequencies to pass. But these are not bandpass and thus would not respond to specific temporal frequencies with great
precision. Can this be explained more?
5. Lines 281-288 mention the advantage of each frame encoding a time-weighted history of motion trajectories. This is
standard in all DVS + neuromorphic vision systems. See Fig. 2 in "HOTS: A Hierarchy of Event-Based Time-Surfaces for
Pattern Recognition" (https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7508476) for an example. This is a direct benefit of any system
that appends an exponential decay kernel to visual events and is not a novel/unexpected result presented by this work.
Learning systems that train on DVS hardware data (with exponential decay kernel circuits or similar downstream processing
in software) are highly competent at next-frame prediction of complex trajectories, required, for example, in optical flow tasks.
6. For the last section, titled “Demonstration of neuromorphic fusion imaging,” it is likely that a DVS-only or DVS + RGB input
would yield a better result than the provided conventional imaging hardware result. It would be a fairer comparison since
DVS hardware data: (1) is better suited for hazy conditions and (2) can have built-in exponential decay kernel circuitry that

used for the photosynapse array hardware -- for the DVS hardware data. In this way, the learning models would be of
comparable size/capacity, incurring comparable energy consumption, but would be tailored to their specific input data.
